## 1 Introduction

The _(worst-case) sensitivity_ of an algorithm is the maximum change in its output, measured in Hamming distance, when a single input element is perturbed. For randomized algorithms we compare output distributions using earth mover’s distance (EMD). Sensitivity offers a foundational robustness metric for algorithms and has deep connections to sublinear-time and distributed computation \[15\]. Sensitivity also underpins consistent decision making and reproducible knowledge discovery. Prior work has developed low-sensitivity algorithms for numerous combinatorial optimization problems \[31, 32, 45, 47, 48\], clustering tasks \[34, 39, 46\], and decision tree learning \[25\].

On the lower-bound side, it is known that computing 2-coloring of a bipartite graph requires sensitivity \(\Omega(n)\) \[45\]. Recently, Fleming and Yoshida \[15\] leveraged probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs) to show that, for canonical constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) such as Max E3SAT, Max E3LIN2, and Max Cut, there exist constants \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) for which any \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithm must have sensitivity \(\Omega(n^\delta)\), where _n_ denotes the number of variables or vertices. Standard reductions then yield \(\Omega(n^\delta)\) lower bounds for approximation algorithms for the maximum clique and minimum vertex cover problems. While their framework provides the first nontrivial lower bounds for approximation algorithms, it nevertheless has several shortcomings:

• The \(\Omega(n^\delta)\) sensitivity bound is evidently far from tight.<tbc>

• The lower bounds for Max E3LIN2 and Max Cut are obtained via gadget reductions from Max E3SAT, so they say nothing about approximation algorithms for satisfiable instances.<tbc>

• The argument applies only to worst-case sensitivity, leaving the behavior under randomly chosen perturbations unresolved.

In this work we address these shortcomings by relating sensitivity to locally testable codes (LTCs) and showing how the existence of an LTC yields sensitivity lower bounds. We outline the framework below.

### 1.1 Our Contributions

#### Sensitivity Lower Bounds for CSPs via LTCs.

_Locally testable codes (LTCs)_ \[22\] are error- correcting codes whose membership can be checked by probing only a constant number of coordinates of the received word. An LTC is called a _strong LTC_ \[21\] if there exists \(\kappa>0\) such that the rejection probability is at least \(\kappa\) times the relative distance from the code. The parameter \(\kappa\) is called the _detection probability_ of the code. As we only consider strong LTCs in this work, we also call them LTCs. In this work, we mainly consider linear codes, meaning they form a subspace of \(\mathbb{F}_p^n\).

An LTC naturally induces a CSP instance: we regard each coordinate of the input word as a variable, and each test performed by the tester as a constraint on those variables. The _variable degree_ \(\theta\) of the tester is the maximum number of constraints that query any single coordinate. If the input is a codeword the instance is satisfiable, whereas inputs far from the code violate a fraction of the constraints that is proportional to their distance from the code. For an LTC _C_, let MaxCSP(_C_) denote the Max CSP whose constraints are restricted to those used in the tester for _C_. Throughout the introduction, we measure sensitivity for CSP instances with respect to deleting a single constraint. The main contribution of this work is showing a general scheme that converts a linear LTC _C_ to a sensitivity lower bound of MaxCSP(_C_).

<tbc>**Theorem 1.1.** _Let_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _and C be a linear LTC over_ F_<sub>p</sub> of block length n, relative distance_ \(\delta\)_, rate r, variable degree_ \(\theta\)_, with detection probability_ \(\kappa\)_. Then, any_ \((1-\varepsilon)\)_-approximation algorithm for_ MaxCSP(_C_) _has sensitivity at least_

\(\frac{n}{2\theta}\left(\delta\left(1-\frac{p}{p-1}\frac{\varepsilon}{r\kappa}\right)-\frac{2\varepsilon}{\kappa}\right)-\frac{1}{2\theta}.\)

_even on satisfiable instances._

We emphasize that this lower bound is information-theoretic and does not rely on any complexity assumption.

We first instantiate Theorem 1.1 using the _c_<sup>3</sup>-LTC of \[12, 38\], which enjoys constant relative distance, constant rate, a constant number of queries, and constant detection probability. The associated CSP is Max E3LIN2, whose constraints are linear equations of the form _x+y+z=b_ over F<sub>2</sub>.

**Theorem 1.2.** _There exists_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _such that every_ \((1-\varepsilon)\)_-approximation algorithm for Max E3LIN2 must have sensitivity_ \(\Omega(n)\) _even when the input instances are satisfiable._

Since the assignment length is _n_, every algorithm automatically has sensitivity at most _n_, so Theorem 1.2 matches this trivial upper bound up to the hidden constant. Equivalently, for satisfiable Max E3LIN2, even slightly stable algorithms cannot achieve a \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation.

Previously, the best lower bound was \(\Omega(n^\delta)\) for some \(\delta>0\), and it applied only to arbitrary (not necessarily satisfiable) instances \[15\]. This non-tight exponent comes from the PCP-based reduction: it blows an _n_-variable instance up to size about \(N:=n^{1/\delta}\), so even if the \(\Omega(n)\) sensitivity lower bound survives the reduction, expressing the result in terms of the enlarged instance size _N_ leaves only an \(\Omega(N^\delta)\) lower bound.

Via standard reductions from Max E3LIN2 to Max 3SAT and Max Cut (see, e.g., \[44\]), we can show that \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithms for Max E3SAT must have sensitivity \(\Omega(n)\) even on satisfiable instances, and that \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithms for Max Cut on general graphs incur sensitivity \(\Omega(n)\) as well. These results again improve upon the prior sensitivity bound of \(\Omega(n^\delta)\) \[15\].

To derive a sensitivity bound specific to Max Cut on bipartite graphs, we construct an LTC whose associated CSP is precisely Max Cut and substitute it into Theorem 1.1. The result is striking because it holds even on bipartite inputs, where a perfect cut always exists:

**Theorem 1.3.** _There exists a constant_ \(\varepsilon_0>0\) _such that for every even n and every_ \(0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0/\sqrt{n}\)_, any_ \((1-\varepsilon)\)_-approximation algorithm for Max Cut on bipartite graphs on n vertices must have sensitivity_ \(\Omega(1/\varepsilon)\).

Thus even on this highly structured class, where the optimum cut is trivial, any near-optimal algorithm must make \(\Omega(1/\varepsilon)\) changes after a single edge deletion. As we mentioned, it was known that any algorithm for 2-coloring a bipartite graph requires \(\Omega(n)\) sensitivity \[45\], which matches the regime \(\varepsilon<1/n\) in Theorem 1.3. Our result generalizes this by showing an \(\Omega(1/\varepsilon)\) sensitivity bound for all \(\varepsilon\) as large as \(\Theta(1/\sqrt{n})\).

## Sensitivity Lower Bounds for Other Combinatorial Problems.

Applying the standard FGLSS reduction \[14\] together with the serial repetition to Theorem 1.2, as in \[15\], yields the following lower bound for the maximum clique problem. Here, we consider the setting that the algorithm outputs a vertex set that forms a clique, and sensitivity is measured with respect to deleting a single edge.

**Theorem 1.4.** _Let_ \(\varepsilon>0\)_. Then, any algorithm for the maximum clique problem that outputs an_ \(n^{-\varepsilon}\)_-approximate clique with probability_ 1-_O_(1_/n_) _must have sensitivity_ \(\Omega(n^{1-c\varepsilon})\) _for some universal constant c\>_0.

Consider the naive (and inefficient) strategy that computes the maximum clique and then truncates it to size at most \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\). This procedure achieves an \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) approximation with sensitivity \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\), and Theorem 1.4 shows that this dependence is essentially optimal. Also, the previous lower bound \[15\] shows that there exist _some_ constants \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) such that any \(n^{-\varepsilon}\)-approximation algorithm has sensitivity \(\Omega(n^\delta)\). By contrast, our lower bound of \(\Omega(n^{1-c\varepsilon})\) holds for _any_ \(\varepsilon>0\).

We also study the _maximum k-coverage problem_, where an instance consists of a universe _U_ and a family F of subsets of _U_. The goal is to select a subfamily \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\) of _k_ sets that covers as many elements as possible. Sensitivity is measured with respect to deleting a single element from _U_ (and removing it from every set in F). Via a reduction from Max E3SAT we derive the following:

**Theorem 1.5.** _There exists_ \(\varepsilon_0>0\) _such that, for every_ \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0\) _and_ \(k<1/(2\varepsilon)\)_, any_ \((1-\varepsilon)\)_- approximation algorithm for the maximum k-coverage problem must have sensitivity_ \(\Omega(k)\)_, even when the instance admits a solution that covers all elements with k sets._

Observe that any algorithm for the maximum _k_-coverage problem has sensitivity at most _k_, since its output contains at most _k_ sets. Thus Theorem 1.5 shows that even permitting a slight approximation does not improve over this trivial upper bound. We also note that, combining the prior \(\Omega(n^\delta)\) lower bound for Max E3SAT \[15\] with the same reduction yields only \(\Omega(k/n^{1-\delta})\), which is negligible. Achieving a linear lower bound is therefore essential.

## Boolean-Function Consequences.

The LTC construction behind Theorem 1.2 also gives a Boolean-function barrier for satisfiable Max E3SAT. Under the standard reduction, each message \(m\in\{0,1\}^k\) indexes a formula \(\Phi(m)\) in an explicit satisfiable family, and flipping one message bit changes only _O_(1) clauses. Composing a randomized approximation algorithm with the map \(m\mapsto\Phi(m)\) and then fixing its internal randomness turns each output bit into a Boolean function on {0,1}_<sup>k</sup>_. The _influence_ of an output bit is the expected number of message coordinates whose flip changes that bit, equivalently, the expected number of adjacent formulas \(\Phi(m)\) and \(\Phi(m^{\oplus i})\) on which that output bit differs. Our sensitivity lower bound therefore implies that, averaged over the internal randomness, linearly many output coordinates have influence \(\Omega(k)\):

**Theorem 1.6** (Informal version of Corollary 6.3)**.** _There is an explicit bounded-occurrence family of satisfiable Max E3SAT formulas on_ \(n=\Theta(k)\) _variables such that, for every such randomized algorithm, averaged over the internal randomness, linearly many output bits have influence_ \(\Omega(k)\).

Friedgut’s junta theorem and Hatami’s pseudo-junta theorem \[16, 28\] show that small total influence forces strong structural simplification. Our theorem therefore implies that linearly many output bits stay a constant distance away from all small juntas and pseudo-juntas (Corollary 6.6). It also implies that linearly many output coordinates have linear decision-tree depth (Corollary 6.7). Likewise, average-sensitivity bounds of Boppana and Rossman \[5, 41\] yield lower bounds for randomized polynomial-size constant-depth circuits (that is, randomized _AC_<sup>0</sup>) and randomized bounded-depth formulas (Corollary 6.8).

Unlike previous lower bounds for random _k_-SAT, including the bounded-depth _decision_ lower bound of Gamarnik, Mossel, and Zadik and the low-degree-polynomial _search_ lower bound of Bresler and Huang \[7, 18\], these lower bounds apply to an explicit satisfiable Max E3SAT family and rule out randomized _AC_<sup>0</sup> circuits and bounded-depth formulas for producing near-satisfying assignments even when the algorithm may output any of many near-optimal assignments.

### Locality Lower Bounds for the Non-signaling Model.

Our sensitivity bounds remain strong even in the non-signaling model, which strictly generalizes classical LOCAL, quantum-LOCAL, and bounded-dependence models: satisfiable Max E3LIN2 still requires locality \(\Omega(logn)\), and bipartite Max Cut requires locality \(\Omega(log(1/\varepsilon))\).

In the _non-signaling model_ \[1, 2, 11, 20\], given a graph _G_=(_V,E_), we can produce an arbitrary output distribution as long as it does not violate the non-signaling principle: for any set of vertices \(S\subseteq V\) , modifying the structure of the input graph at more than a distance _t_ from _S_ does not affect the output distribution of _S_. The parameter _t_ is called the _locality_ of the model. This model is stronger than any "physical" synchronous distributed computing model, and in particular, it contains classical LOCAL \[35\], quantum-LOCAL \[20\], and the bounded-dependence model \[29\]. Consequently, any locality lower bound in the non-signaling model applies automatically to these models.

The following observation from \[15\] connects locality to sensitivity. Suppose we generate a distribution in the non-signaling model for a graph problem with locality _t_. Sampling from this distribution and outputting the result yields an algorithm whose sensitivity is \(O(\Delta^t)\), where \(\Delta\) denotes the maximum degree, because deleting an edge can affect the marginal distributions of at most \(\Delta^t\) vertices. Because the CSP instance produced by the _c_<sup>3</sup>-LTC \[12, 38\] has constant degree, Theorem 1.2 translates into the following lower bound:

**Theorem 1.7.** _There exists_ \(\varepsilon>0\) _such that any_ \((1-\varepsilon)\)_-approximate non-signaling distribution for Max E3LIN2 must have locality_ \(\Omega(logn)\)_, even on satisfiable instances._

Marwaha and Hadfield \[36\] showed that achieving a \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation on satisfiable instances already requires \(\Omega(logn)\) rounds in quantum-LOCAL, and Fleming and Yoshida \[15\] proved the same locality bound in the non-signaling model for general instances. Our theorem unifies these results by establishing that even satisfiable Max E3LIN2 instances demand \(\Omega(logn)\) locality for non-signaling distributions.

Similarly, Theorem 1.3 yields the following lower bound for the non-signaling model:

**Theorem 1.8.** _There exists a constant_ \(\varepsilon_0>0\) _such that for every even n and every_ \(0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0/\sqrt{n}\)_, any_ \((1-\varepsilon)\)_-approximate non-signaling distribution for the maximum cut problem on bipartite graphs must have locality_ \(\Omega(log(1/\varepsilon))\).

Hence setting \(\varepsilon=n^{-\delta}\) for any small constant \(\delta>0\) forces locality \(\Omega(logn)\). The previously best locality barrier on bipartite graphs is that any _one-round_ quantum-LOCAL algorithm achieves at most a \((\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2d}})\)-approximation on _d_-regular bipartite graphs \[3\]. No stronger locality lower bound was known that rules out \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximations on bipartite inputs, even for LOCAL.

On general graphs, there exist \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithms in LOCAL (and even CONGEST) that run in \(O(poly(1/\varepsilon)\cdot logn)\) rounds \[9\]. By contrast, Fleming and Yoshida \[15\] showed an \(\Omega(logn)\) locality lower bound in the non-signaling model for achieving \((1-\varepsilon)\) approximation for some \(\varepsilon>0\).

## 1.2 Proof Overview

We first sketch the argument underlying Theorem 1.1 and then outline how it yields Theorems 1.2 and 1.3.

### An analogy between optimization problems and systematic LTCs.

We exploit a tight parallel between optimization problems and systematic LTCs, where _systematic_ means that the encoder copies the _k_ message symbols verbatim into designated coordinates, inducing a canonical input/output split. We write \(x\sim x'\) for neighboring instances.

Consider an optimization problem with input space I, output space O, and evaluation map \(e:\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{O}\rightarrow[0,1]\). A deterministic \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithm \(\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{I}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}\) satisfies \(e(x,\mathcal{A}(x))\in[1-\varepsilon,1]\) for every _x_. Attaching the input to the output, \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(x)=(x,\mathcal{A}(x))\), yields the diagram

\(\mathcal{I}-\rightarrow^\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{O}-\rightarrow^e[1-\varepsilon,1].\)

The sensitivity of A is the maximum, over neighboring inputs \(x\sim x'\), of the distance between \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(x)\) and \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(x')\) inside \(\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{O}\). To derive a lower bound we therefore search for neighboring inputs that force any \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithm to output points that are well separated for at least two inputs in \(\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{O}\), mirroring the coding-theoretic requirement that distinct messages map to distant codewords.

Now replace the algorithm by a systematic LTC _C_ with an encoder _f_. Let _n_ be the block length, _k_ be the message length, \(\delta\) be the relative distance, and _T_ be the tester with detection probability \(\kappa\). Then, define _e(x_)=**Pr**\[_T_ accepts _x_\]. Every codeword _f(m_) for a message _m_ satisfies _e(m,f(m_))=1, so we obtain the analogous diagram

\(\Sigma^k-\rightarrow^f\Sigma^k\times\Sigma^{n-k}-\rightarrow^e\{1\}.\)

Because the code has relative distance \(\delta\), distinct messages map to codewords whose relative Hamming distance is at least \(\delta\), mirroring the separation requirement for optimization algorithms.

To reason about approximate outputs we invoke strong testability. Think of _f_ as an exact algorithm that always attains the optimum 1 of _e_. If another encoder B satisfies \(e(m,\mathcal{B}(m))\ge 1-\varepsilon\), strong testability guarantees that \(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}(m)\) lies within distance \(\varepsilon/\kappa\) of some codeword. Consequently we get the diagram

\(\Sigma^k-\rightarrow^\tilde{\mathcal{B}}\Sigma^k\times\Sigma^{n-k}-\rightarrow^e[1-\varepsilon,1].\)

The distance between the codewords of neighboring messages \(m\sim m'\) therefore forces a comparable separation between \(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}(m)\) and \(\tilde{\mathcal{B}}(m')\), yielding the desired sensitivity lower bound.

The systematic nature of the code is crucial: it embeds the message directly into the codeword, so the tester _T_ enforces consistency between input and output rather than merely checking membership in the code.

## Any approximate encoder has high sensitivity.

With this analogy in place we outline how to prove the sensitivity lower bound for approximation algorithms on the induced CSP, thereby establishing Theorem 1.1. Fix a randomized \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithm A for MaxCSP(_C_). Given a message _m_, we construct a CSP instance I_<sub>C</sub>(m_) that is satisfiable exactly by the codeword for _m_, and strong testability ensures that the output of \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\) on I_<sub>C</sub>(m_) lies within Hamming distance \(\varepsilon/\kappa\) of that codeword. Hence we may view \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\) as an approximate encoder that attempts to extend _m_. To force large sensitivity we must find neighboring messages \(m\sim m'\) whose outputs fall into balls centred at different codewords. To this end we introduce the nearest-message decoder \(\sigma:\Sigma^n\rightarrow\Sigma^k\) and show that for some \(m\sim m'\) the values \(\sigma\circ\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m))\) and \(\sigma\circ\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m'))\) differ with constant probability; by the code’s relative distance this forces \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m))\) and \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m'))\) to have large earth mover’s distance.

However, it is not enough to focus on a single pair \(m\sim m'\): the encoder \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\) might always output the codeword for _m_, achieving zero sensitivity while staying nearly optimal for _m_ and \(m'\). Instead we average over all such pairs. For any approximate encoder \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\) we define a functional _L_ that averages the earth mover’s distance between \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m))\) and \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m'))\) across all \(m\sim m'\). This functional lower bounds the worst-case sensitivity and, more strongly, the average sensitivity under uniformly random constraint deletions.

The difficulty is that A can otherwise be arbitrary. Yet _L_ is convex, so we may symmetrize \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\) by averaging over permutations of message coordinates and alphabet symbols without increasing _L_. Composing the symmetrized encoder \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\) with the nearest-message decoder \(\sigma\) produces, for each message _m_, a distribution \(\nu_m^*\) over \(\Sigma^k\) whose probabilities depend only on the Hamming distance to _m_, making the analysis tractable. We then show that some neighboring pair \(m\sim m'\) forces \(\sigma\circ\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m))\) and \(\sigma\circ\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m'))\) to differ with constant probability, yielding the desired sensitivity lower bound.

### Sensitivity lower bounds from explicit LTCs

Given the connection between sensitivity lower bounds and LTCs, we instantiate our framework with two explicit families. First, we adapt the left-right Cayley complex (LRCC) codes of Dinur, Evra, Livne, Lubotzky, and Mozes \[12\] into systematic LTCs whose induced CSP is Max E3LIN2. This transformation preserves their rate, distance, and detection probability, letting us transfer the _c_<sup>3</sup>-LTC guarantees and derive \(\Omega(n)\) average-sensitivity lower bounds for every \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithm, thereby proving Theorem 1.2.

Second, we analyze signed repetition codes that duplicate each message coordinate alongside its complement. We partition the coordinates into _A_ (original copies) and _B_ (flipped copies), embed a bipartite expander on \(A\cup B\), and use a two-query tester that checks random edges for disagreement, thereby realizing a Max Cut instance. The replication factor controls both the rate and distance, and feeding this construction into our framework establishes Theorem 1.3.

## 1.3 Related Work and Discussion

### Max Cut.

It is natural to ask whether one can beat the sensitivity lower bound of Theorem 1.3 by applying Theorem 1.1 to a different two-query LTC. However, in such a tester, every constraint enforces that a pair of queried coordinates differs, so codewords correspond exactly to 2-colorings of the tester’s constraint graph. The number of codewords, and hence the rate, is dictated by the number of connected components, while the minimum distance is governed by the sizes of those components. Consequently, an LTC obtained this way cannot simultaneously achieve high rate and large distance, preventing stronger lower bounds via this route.

### Lower Bounds for Other CSPs.

For a linear code _C_, MaxCSP(_C_) necessarily collapses to a system of linear equations. Attempts to extend our lower bounds via gadget reductions such as pp-definitions or pp-interpretations \[4, 8\] stall here: starting from linear equations one cannot reach target languages whose expressive power is incomparable with (or weaker than) linear systems, so reductions to templates like 2SAT or Horn-SAT are ruled out. Another idea is to replace LTCs with dictatorship tests from the PCP literature \[27, 30\], but it remains unclear whether such tests can be adapted to yield sensitivity lower bounds.

### Machine Unlearning

_(Exact) machine unlearning_ is often formalized by requiring that, after deleting a data item, the algorithm’s output matches the model one would obtain by retraining on the pruned dataset \[6, 24, 37\]. Viewed through this lens, our sensitivity lower bounds translate directly into recourse lower bounds for unlearning. In particular, Theorem 1.5 shows that for the maximum _k_-coverage problem--a canonical abstraction for summarization and selection tasks--the deletion of a single universe element forces any exact-unlearning mechanism that maintains a \((1-\varepsilon)\)- approximation to modify \(\Omega(k)\) members of the selected set family to match the retrained solution. Hence exact unlearning cannot rely on small, local "patches": even a single deletion necessitates wholesale restructuring of the learned summary.

### Sensitivity on Planar Graphs

The constraint graph of a 2CSP instance has one vertex per variable and an edge for each constraint connecting the variables it involves. Our results establish lower bounds for the class of constraint graphs induced by the LTCs we employ; for instance, the repetition code we use for Max Cut yields an expander constraint graph.

A natural question is whether algorithms with low (average) sensitivity exist for non-expanding graphs such as planar ones. When the planar graph also has bounded degree, the partition oracle \[26, 33\] gives a \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximate Max Cut algorithm with average sensitivity \(\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)\) under vertex deletions. However, it remains unclear whether an analogous guarantee holds for general planar graphs, where the maximum degree may be unbounded. For the lower-bound side, an LTC whose Tanner graph is planar and has rate \(\ge 5/8\) must have distance _O_(1_/n_) \[43\]. Consequently, applying Theorem 1.1 to planar graphs would require LTCs of smaller rate.

### Overlap Gap Property.

The _overlap gap property (OGP)_ is a geometric/topological description of near-optimal solution spaces: in many random optimization problems, the set of \((1-\varepsilon)\)-optimal solutions splits into clusters whose pairwise overlaps avoid a nontrivial interval. OGP has emerged as a unifying explanation for barriers for local algorithms in high-dimensional random structures \[10, 19\] and is surveyed by Gamarnik, who frames it as a topological obstruction to optimization \[17\]. Classical OGP analyzes overlaps between near-optimal solutions on the same instance (or across randomly coupled instances), whereas our sensitivity framework compares outputs of algorithms on two almost-identical instances. At a high level the direction is similar: both aim to rule out stable/local algorithms, i.e., OGP via geometric gaps in the near-optimal solution space, and our results via explicit worst-case instances where tiny input perturbations force large output changes.

### Circuit-complexity lower bounds for SAT and related search problems.

For unrestricted circuits, lower bounds for _search_-SAT are closely connected to lower bounds for _decision_-SAT: Pich proved implications between formalized search and decision lower-bound principles \[40\]. Because such general lower bounds remain out of reach, known assumption-free results mostly concern restricted models, on both the decision and the search side. On the decision side, Gamarnik, Mossel, and Zadik proved that depth-_d_ bounded-depth circuits for random 2-SAT near the satisfiability threshold require size \(\mathrm{exp}(n^{\Theta(1/d)})\) \[18\]. On the search side, Bresler and Huang showed that low-degree polynomial algorithms cannot find satisfying assignments for random _k_-SAT at clause densities of order 2_<sup>k</sup>_log_k/k_, excluding a broad family of algorithms, including local methods and several message-passing procedures \[7\]. In a different restricted model, Göös, Kamath, Robere, and Sokolov proved exponential monotone circuit lower bounds for a monotone variant of XOR-SAT \[23\]. By contrast, our results give a lower bound for randomized bounded-depth circuits and formulas for producing near-satisfying assignments on an explicit satisfiable Max E3SAT family, rather than an average-case decision lower bound for random formulas or a lower bound in a different restricted search model.

## 2 Preliminaries

For a positive integer _n_, let \[_n_\] denote the set {1,2_,...,n_}. For two strings \(x,y\in\Sigma^n\), we write _x∼y_ when they differ on exactly one coordinate. Also, we write \(d_\mathrm{H}(x,y):=\#\{i\in[n]:x_i\neq y_i\}\) for the _(unnormalized) Hamming distance_ and \(\delta_\mathrm{H}(x,y):=d_\mathrm{H}(x,y)/n\) for its normalized/relative version. Note that we use the relative Hamming distance only in the context of error-correcting codes. To avoid tedious transforms between normalized Hamming distances with different denominators, we always use the block length _n_ of the code as the denominator when dealing with codes.

## 2.1 Sensitivity

Let \((\Omega,d)\) be a finite metric space and let \(\mu,\nu\) be distributions over \(\Omega\). The _earth mover’s distance_ between \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) is

\(\mathsf{EMD}_d(\mu,\nu):=inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\sum_{x,y\in\Omega} d(x,y)\pi(x,y),\)

where \(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) denotes the set of all couplings of \(\mu\) and \(\nu\). When the metric is clear from context we write simply \(\mathsf{EMD}(\mu,\nu)\). If _d_ is the discrete metric on \(\Omega\), i.e., _d(x,y_)=1 when \(x\neq y\) and 0 otherwise, then \(\mathsf{EMD}_d(\mu,\nu)=\mathsf{TV}(\mu,\nu)\), the total variation distance between \(\mu\) and \(\nu\).

Consider a problem in which an input instance _I_ consists of elements _e_<sub>1</sub>_,...,e<sub>n</sub>_ and the output space is a metric space \((\Omega,d)\). For an element \(e\in I\), let _I-e_ denote the instance obtained by deleting _e_. The _sensitivity_ of a (possibly randomized) algorithm A at _I_ is

\(\mathsf{Sens}(\mathcal{A},I):=max_{i\in[n]}\mathsf{EMD}_d(\mathcal{A}(I),\mathcal{A}(I-e_i)),\)

where we identify A(_I_) with its output distribution.

## 2.2 Locally Testable s

For \(w\in\Sigma^n\) and a subset \(C\subseteq\Sigma^n\), we set \(\delta_\mathrm{H}(w,C):=min_{c\in C}\delta_\mathrm{H}(w,c)\).

**Definition 2.1** (Error-correcting code)**.** Let \(n,k\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(n\ge k\) and let \(\Sigma\) be a finite alphabet. A _(block) error-correcting code_ of length _n_ and message length _k_ over \(\Sigma\) is a pair (_C,f_), where \(C\subseteq\Sigma^n\) and the encoder \(f:\Sigma^k\rightarrow C\) is a bijection. The _rate_ of the code is _r=k/n_, and its _(relative) distance_ is \(min_{c,c^\prime\in C,c\neq c^\prime}\delta_\mathrm{H}(c,c')\). We often identify the code with the subset _C_ when the encoder is clear from context.

**Definition 2.2** (Linear code)**.** A code (_C,f_) over F_<sub>p</sub>_ is _linear_ if _C_ is a linear subspace of \(\mathbb{F}_p^n\), equivalently if _f_ is a linear map. The (absolute) distance of a linear code equals the minimum Hamming weight of a nonzero codeword.

**Definition 2.3** (Locally testable codes)**.** Let \(r,\delta,\kappa\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), \(q,\theta\in\mathbb{N}\). We say an error-correcting code (_C,f_) is a _locally testable code_ (LTC) with detection probability \(\kappa\), _q_ queries, and variable degree \(\theta\) if the following properties hold:

• There exists a collection S of _q_-subsets of \[_n_\] such that each subset _S_ is associated with a set \(V_S\subseteq\Sigma^S\) called _allowed local views_, satisfying \(c|_S\in V_S\) for all \(c\in C\), and<tbc>

<tbc>\(\forall w\in\Sigma^n:\mathbf{Pr}_{S\sim\mathcal{S}}\left[w|_S\notin V_S\right]\ge\kappa\cdot\delta_\mathrm{H}(w,C),\)<tbc>

<tbc>where _S_∼S denotes the uniform distribution over S.<tbc>

• For any \(i\in[n]\), we have \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\unknown\left[i\in S\right]\le\theta\).

When we need to emphasize the local tests, we denote the LTC by \((C,f,\mathcal{S},\mathcal{V})\), where \(\mathcal{V}=\{V_S\}_{S\in\mathcal{S}}\).

**Definition 2.4** (Systematic code)**.** Let \(n,k\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(n\ge k\) and let \(\Sigma\) be a finite alphabet. Let \(\pi:\Sigma^n\rightarrow\Sigma^k\) be the projection onto the first _k_ coordinates. A _systematic code_ of length _n_ and message length _k_ over \(\Sigma\) is an error-correcting code (_C,f_) with an encoder \(f:\Sigma^k\rightarrow\Sigma^n\) such that \(\pi\circ f=\mathrm{id}_{\Sigma^k}\). Thus the message _x_ appears verbatim as the first _k_ entries of the codeword _f(x_). We also say that a code \(C\subseteq\Sigma^n\) is _systematic_ if it admits such an encoder.

The next lemma shows that any linear locally testable code becomes systematic after permuting coordinates. The proof is deferred to Appendix A.

**Lemma 2.5.** _If_ \(C\subseteq\mathbb{F}_p^n\) _is a linear LTC, then there exists a permutation matrix_ \(\Pi\) _such that_ \(\Pi C\) _is a systematic LTC with the same parameters._

### 2.3 Constraint Satisfaction Problems

Let _V_ be a finite set of variables and let \(\Sigma\) be a finite alphabet. An instance of a _constraint satisfaction problem (CSP)_ over \(\Sigma\) is a tuple \((V,\Sigma,\mathcal{C})\), where C is a finite collection of constraints. Each constraint is given by a pair (_S,R_) with \(S\subseteq V\) its scope and \(R\subseteq\Sigma^S\) the set of allowed local assignments. An assignment \(\alpha\in\Sigma^V\) _satisfies_ (_S,R_) if \(\alpha|_S\in R\), and it is a solution to the instance when it satisfies every constraint in C. The associated _maximum constraint satisfaction problem (Max CSP)_ asks for an assignment \(\alpha\in\Sigma^V\) that maximizes the number of satisfied constraints.

For a CSP instance \(\mathcal{I}=(V,\Sigma,\mathcal{C})\) and a constraint \(c\in\mathcal{C}\), we write I-_c_ for the instance obtained by removing _c_ from C.

## 3 Sensitivity Lower Bounds via LTCs

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 1.1. We organize the argument in four stages. First, Section 3.1 shows how a systematic LTC induces a CSP whose constraints mirror the tester. Next, in Section 3.2 we discuss the nearest-message decoder, which recovers the planted message from near-optimal assignments, and accompanying stability bounds. Building on these tools, Section 3.3 symmetrizes the decoder’s output distributions and proves a large total-variation gap between neighboring messages. Finally, Section 3.4 converts this gap into an earth mover’s distance lower bound for worst-case sensitivity, and the same argument also yields an average-sensitivity analogue, giving Theorem 1.1.

### 3.1 CSP Induced by an LTC

For \(m\in\Sigma^k\) and a subset \(U\subseteq\Sigma^{n-k}\), we write \(m\oplus U:=\{(m,u):u\in U\}\subseteq\Sigma^n\).

**Definition 3.2.** For a systematic LTC _C_, we define an optimization problem MaxCSP(_C_) as follows. The input is a message \(m\in\Sigma^k\), and the goal is to compute an assignment in \(\Sigma^V\) that maximizes the number of satisfied constraints in I_<sub>C</sub>(m_).

Notice that all constraints in I_<sub>C</sub>(m_) can be satisfied by assigning the code bits of _f(m_) to the variables.

## 3.2 Nearest-Message Decoder

We collect here the decoder and stability statements that connect near-optimal assignments to nearby codewords.

**Definition 3.3.** Let \(\sigma:\Sigma^n\rightarrow\Sigma^k\) be the _nearest-message decoder_ for (_C,f_), that is, for every \(w\in\Sigma^n\) the value \(\sigma(w)\) belongs to

\(argmin_{m^\prime\in\Sigma^k}\delta_\mathrm{H}\left(f(m'),w\right).\)

We break ties arbitrarily.

**Lemma 3.4.** _Let C be a systematic LTC with rate r=k/n and let_ A _be an_ \((1-\varepsilon)\)_-approximation randomized algorithm for_ MaxCSP(_C). Then for every_ \(m\in\Sigma^k\),<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}\big[\delta_\mathrm{H}(\sigma(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m))),m)\big]\le\frac{\varepsilon}{\kappa}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Because A achieves approximation ratio \(1-\varepsilon\), the expected fraction of satisfied constraints on the instance I_<sub>C</sub>(m_) is at least \(1-\varepsilon\), whence<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\#\text{of unsatisfied constraints in}\mathcal{I}_C(m)}{|\mathcal{C}|}\right]\le\varepsilon.\)

<tbc>For every word \(w\in\Sigma^n\), Definition 2.3 guarantees that the rejection probability is at least \(\kappa\cdot\delta_\mathrm{H}(w,C)\). Applying this to the random output \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m))\) gives

\(\frac{\#\text{of unsatisfied constraints in}\mathcal{I}_C(m)}{|\mathcal{C}|}\ge\kappa\cdot\delta_\mathrm{H}(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m)),C).\)

Taking expectations yields \(\mathbb{E}[\delta_\mathrm{H}(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m)),C)]\le\varepsilon/\kappa\).

Let \(w:=\tilde{\mathcal{A}}(\mathcal{I}_C(m))\) and let \(c^\star:=f(\sigma(w))\) be the codeword selected by the nearest-message decoder. By definition, \(\delta_\mathrm{H}(w,C)=\delta_\mathrm{H}(w,c^\star)\). Because _f_ is systematic, the first _k_ entries of _w_ coincide with the message _m_, while the first _k_ entries of _c<sup>⋆</sup>_ coincide with \(\sigma(w)\). Consequently every coordinate where \(\sigma(w)\) and _m_ differ must also be a coordinate where _w_ and _c<sup>⋆</sup>_ differ. We therefore have

\(\delta_\mathrm{H}(\sigma(w),m)\le\delta_\mathrm{H}(w,c^\star)=\delta_\mathrm{H}(w,C).\)

Taking expectations over the randomness of \(\tilde{\mathcal{A}}\) completes the proof.

\(\mathrm{max}\big\{\mathsf{EMD}_{\delta_\mathrm{H}}\big(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{I}^{(j^\star-1)}),\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{I}^{(j^\star)})\big),\mathsf{EMD}_{\delta_\mathrm{H}}\big(\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{I}'^{(j^\star-1)}),\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{I}'^{(j^\star)})\big)\big\}\ge\frac{1}{2\theta}\left(\delta\left(1-\frac{p}{p-1}\frac{\varepsilon}{r\kappa}\right)-\frac{2\varepsilon}{\kappa}-\frac{1}{n}\right).\)

Because \(\delta_\mathrm{H}=d_\mathrm{H}/n\), multiplying by _n_ converts this to the unnormalized Hamming metric. Hence there exists a satisfiable instance witnessing worst-case sensitivity at least

\(\frac{n}{2\theta}\left(\delta\left(1-\frac{p}{p-1}\frac{\varepsilon}{r\kappa}\right)-\frac{2\varepsilon}{\kappa}\right)-\frac{1}{2\theta},\)

## 4 Sensitivity Lower Bounds from Explicit LTCs

This section instantiates the abstract sensitivity framework developed in Section 3. We plug explicit families of locally testable codes into Theorem 1.1 to derive sensitivity lower bounds for Max E3LIN2 and Max Cut.

### 4.1 LRCC s and Max E3LIN2

In this section, we present our construction of a systematic LTC whose local tests are parity constraints on constantly many variables. Our construction is based on the _left-right Cayley complex (LRCC) code_ introduced by \[12\], with the concrete construction as in Sections 5 and 6 in \[12\].

**Lemma 4.1** (Theorem 1.1 in \[12\])**.** _For every_ 0_\<r\<_1_, there exist_ \(\delta,\kappa>0\), \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_0\)_, and an infinite family of LTCs_ {_C<sub>n</sub>_} _with rate r, distance_ \(\delta\)_, detection probability_ \(\kappa\)_, and query complexity q._

**Remark 4.2.** Section 5 of \[12\] shows that the codes in Lemma 4.1 are linear over the binary field F<sub>2</sub>.

For completeness we recall the notation surrounding the left-right Cayley complex associated with the codes _C<sub>n</sub>_. Given such a code, let _X_ denote its LRCC, a 2-dimensional simplicial complex. We write \(X(\ell)\) for the set of \(\ell\)-faces of _X_, so _X_(0) is the set of vertices, _X_(1) the edges, and _X_(2) the 2-faces. For any vertex \(g\in X(0)\), the local view \(X_g\subseteq X(2)\) consists of the 2-faces that contain _g_. The LRCC construction equips each local view _X<sub>g</sub>_ with a small code _C<sub>g</sub>_ obtained by restricting the global code to the coordinates indexed by _X<sub>g</sub>_. With this terminology in place, the local testability guarantee established in \[12\] can be stated as follows:

**Lemma 4.3** (Theorem 4.5 in \[12\])**.** _Let Cn be an arbitrary code in Lemma 4.1, and let X denote its LRCC. Then for any_ \(f:X(2)\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_2\)_, we have_ \(\mathbf{Pr}_{g\in X(0)}\left[f|_{X_g}\notin C_g\right]\ge\kappa\cdot\delta_\mathrm{H}(f,C_n).\) However, the local tests on _Xg_ are systems of linear equations rather than single linear constraints, so we translate them into tests that query a constant number of variables. **Lemma 4.4.** _There exists a family of LTCs_ \(\{\tilde{C}_n\}\) _with constant rate, detection probability, distance, variable degree, and query complexity_ 3 _whose local tests are linear equations over_ F2. _Proof._ The codes in Lemma 4.1 are equipped with local tests that evaluate systems of linear equations. To prove the lemma we construct a new family of local tests that 1. consists of individual linear equations (rather than systems of linear equations); and 2. has query complexity 3. We address the two goals steps by step.
**Transform local tests to linear equations.** By the construction of the local low-density parity- check (LDPC) codes (see the proof of Lemma 5.1 in \[12\]), each local code _Cg_ is of the form \(C_0\otimes C_0\) for some LDPC code _C_0. Hence \(f|_{X_g}\in C_g\) if and only if every row and every column of _f|Xg_ lies in _C_0. We view _Xg_ as an \(n_0\times n_0\) grid whose entries correspond to the local coordinates, so each row/column is a subset of _X_(2). Let \(r_{g,1},\dots,r_{g,n_0}\subseteq X(2)\) be these rows and _r__g,n_0+1_,...,r__g,_2_n_0 be the columns. Denote the parity-check matrix of _C_0 by _H_, with rows _h_1_,...,h__k_0. Sample \(g\in X(0)\) uniformly, then sample \(i\in[2n_0]\) and \(j\in[k_0]\) uniformly and independently. Query the coordinates of _f_ indexed by the support of _hj_ inside the row (or column) _rg,i_ and accept iff \(\langle h_j,f|_{r_{g,i}}\rangle=0\). For a fixed _g_, if \(f|_{X_g}\notin C_g\) then some pair (_i,j_) must violate this parity check, so conditioned on such a _g_ the test rejects with probability at least 1/(2_n_0_k_0). Averaging over the random choice of _g_ gives \(\mathbf{Pr}_{g,i,j}\left[\langle h_j,f|_{r_{g,i}}\rangle\neq 0\right]\ge\frac{1}{2n_0k_0}\mathbf{Pr}_{g\in X(0)}\left[f|_{X_g}\notin C_g\right].\) Combining this with the local testability guarantee from Theorem 4.5 of \[12\] yields \(\mathbf{Pr}_{g,i,j}\left[\langle h_j,f|_{r_{g,i}}\rangle\neq 0\right]\ge\frac{\kappa}{2n_0k_0}\delta_\mathrm{H}(f,C_n).\) Each such check touches at most _q_ variables, where _q_ is the query complexity of the base low-density parity-check code _C_0 (Lemma 5.2 of \[12\]). For \(g\in X(0)\), \(i\in[2n_0]\), and \(j\in[k_0]\), let \(S_{g,i,j}\subseteq X(2)\) denote the set of coordinates participating in the parity check \(\langle h_j,f|_{r_{g,i}}\rangle=0\). Let S1 collect all such _Sg,i,j_. The tests in S1 therefore define a new LTC \(\tilde{C}_n\) with local constraints \(\sum_{s\in S_{g,i,j}}x_s=0\text{for every}S_{g,i,j}\in\mathcal{S}_1,\) which coincide with the local checks of the LDPC code _C_0. Because _n_0 and _k_0 are absolute constants, the detection probability \(\kappa':=\kappa/(2n_0k_0)\) is again a constant. The query complexity and variable degree of this test collection are also constant. Indeed, the LDPC code _C_0 has query complexity _q_ and variable degree 7 (Lemma 5.1 of \[12\]). A variable _x_ belongs to _Sg,i,j_ precisely when

1. _x_ is contained in the local view _X<sub>g</sub>_ of the LRCC (there are four such _g_’s),<tbc>

2. _x_ lies in the selected row or column _r<sub>g,i</sub>_ of _X<sub>g</sub>_ (two choices), and<tbc>

3. _x_ participates in the parity check defined by _h<sub>j</sub>_ (at most seven choices).

Therefore each variable participates in at most \(4\cdot 2\cdot 7=56\) tests.

**Reduce the query complexity.** To reduce the query complexity to 3, we apply the standard gadget reduction from EqLIN2 to E3LIN2. For each \(S_{g,i,j}\in\mathcal{S}_1\), denote its indices by _s_<sub>1</sub>_,...,s<sub>q</sub>_. The corresponding local test is the parity constraint<tbc>

\(x_{s_1}+\cdots+x_{s_q}=0.\) (3)

<tbc>Introduce auxiliary variables _y<sub>g,i,j,k</sub>_ for \(2\le k\le q-2\) and replace Equation (3) with the chain

\(\left\{\begin{array}{ c }

y_{g,i,j,2}+x_{s_3}+y_{g,i,j,3}=0, \\

An assignment to \((x_s)_{s\in S_{g,i,j}}\) satisfies Equation (3) if and only if we can extend it to the auxiliary variables so that all constraints in Equation (4) are satisfied. This gadget only blows up the number of tests and the block length by a constant factor, so the rate, distance, detection probability, and variable degree remain constant, while the query complexity drops to 3.

Combining with Theorem 1.1, we immediately get the following.

_Proof of Theorem 1.2._ Let \(\tilde{C}_n\) be the LTCs in Lemma 4.4, whose tests are linear equations. By Lemma 2.5, after a fixed permutation of coordinates we may regard each \(\tilde{C}_n\) as systematic; let _f<sub>n</sub>_ be the corresponding encoders. Then by Definition 3.1, the induced CSP instances of \((\tilde{C}_n,f_n)\) are exactly systems of linear equations on F<sub>2</sub>. and the expression in parentheses is positive for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\) (depending only on the code parameters). Hence the constant hidden in the \(\Omega(\cdot)\) notation depends only on the LTC parameters. This establishes the theorem.

## 4.2 Repetition s and Max Cut

Let _t_ be even, \(A\sqcup B=[t]\) a fixed balanced partition with |_A_|=|_B_|=_t/_2, and \(k\ge 1\). Over the alphabet {0,1} consider the _signed t-fold repetition code_<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Rep}^\pm(k,t)=\left\{y\in\{0,1\}^{tk}:\exists x\in\{0,1\}^k\text{s.t.}y_{a,i}=x_i\forall a\in A,y_{b,i}=1-x_i\forall b\in B,\forall i\in[k]\right\}.\)

Fix any _d_-regular bipartite graph _G_=(_A,B,E_) on the vertex set \(A\cup B\) (|_A_|=|_B_|=_t/_2) and write \(\sigma(G)\in[0,1)\) for the _second singular value_ of its normalized adjacency matrix (equivalently: the largest nontrivial absolute eigenvalue of the random-walk matrix on _G_). Consider the non-adaptive 2-query tester _T_ that, on input \(y\in\{0,1\}^{tk}\),

chooses \(i\in[k]\) uniformly at random, chooses a random edge \((a,b)\in E\), queries the two symbols _y<sub>a,i</sub>,y<sub>b,i</sub>_, and _rejects_ iff _y<sub>a,i</sub>=y<sub>b,i</sub>_.

The blocklength is _n=tk_.

We use the following spectral Poincaré inequality for bipartite _d_-regular graphs.

**Lemma 4.5** (Edge Poincaré)**.** _For any_ \(f:A\cup B\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\),<tbc>

\(\frac{1}{|E|}\sum_{(u,v)\in E}\big(f(u)-f(v)\big)^2\ge 2(1-\sigma(G))\mathrm{Var}(f).\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Let _A<sub>G</sub>_ be the adjacency matrix of _G_ and _P=A<sub>G</sub>/d_. A standard calculation shows

\(\frac{1}{|E|}\sum_{(u,v)\in E}\big(f(u)-f(v)\big)^2=2\big(\langle f,f\rangle-\langle f,Pf\rangle\big).\)

Decompose \(f=\bar{f}\cdot\mathbf{1}+z\) with \(\langle z,\mathbf{1}\rangle=0\). Since **1** is an eigenvector of _P_ with eigenvalue 1 and all other singular values are at most \(\sigma(G)\) in absolute value, \(\langle f,Pf\rangle\le\bar{f}^2+\sigma(G)\langle z,z\rangle\). Thus \(2(\langle f,f\rangle-\langle f,Pf\rangle)\ge 2\big(\langle z,z\rangle-\sigma(G)\langle z,z\rangle\big)=2(1-\sigma(G))\mathrm{Var}(f)\), as claimed.

**Theorem 4.6.** _For the code_ \(\mathrm{Rep}^\pm(k,t)\)_, the following hold:_

1. _The relative distance is_ \(\delta=\frac{1}{k}=\frac{t}{n}\).<tbc>

2. _The rate is_ \(r=\frac{k}{n}=\frac{1}{t}\).<tbc>

_3._ _For every_ \(y\in\{0,1\}^n\),<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathbf{Pr}\left[T\mathrm{rejects}y\right]\ge\kappa\cdot\delta_\mathrm{H}\big(y,\mathrm{Rep}^\pm(k,t)\big),\text{\textit{with}}\kappa=1-\sigma(G).\)<tbc>

<tbc>_In particular,_ \(\kappa\) _is an absolute constant that depends only on d and the expansion of G (and is independent of t and k, hence of the blocklength n)._<tbc>

_4._ _Each coordinate_ (_v,i),_ \(v\in A\cup B\)_, participates in exactly d possible queries (one per incident edge of G). Hence the (maximum) degree is d._

_Proof._ (1)-(2) As in the ordinary repetition code, the encoder \(x\mapsto y\) is injective with message length _k_ and blocklength _n=tk_; two distinct messages differing in one coordinate produce codewords that differ on all _t_ copies of that coordinate, giving minimum (absolute) distance _t_ and relative distance \(\delta=t/n=1/k\).

(3) _Soundness._ Fix a received word _y_ and a column \(i\in[k]\). Define the _flipped_ column \(g_i\in\{0,1\}^{A\cup B}\) by<tbc>

\(g_i(v)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
y_{v,i} & v\in A, \\
1-y_{v,i} & v\in B,
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>so that _g<sub>i</sub>_ is constant iff the _i_-th column of _y_ belongs to the code constraint (_A_-entries equal and _B_- entries their complements). The nearest codeword in column _i_ is obtained by setting all _t_ positions to the majority bit of _g<sub>i</sub>_; hence the per-column contribution to the relative distance is<tbc>

\(\Delta_i=\mathrm{min}\{\mathrm{fractionof}1\text{’s in}g_i,\mathrm{fractionof}0\text{’s in}g_i\}.\)

Note that \(\delta_\mathrm{H}(y,\mathrm{Rep}^\pm(k,t))=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i\).

The tester _T_ samples a random edge \((a,b)\in E\) and rejects iff _y<sub>a,i</sub>=y<sub>b,i</sub>_, which (by construction of _g<sub>i</sub>_) is equivalent to rejecting iff \(g_i(a)\neq g_i(b)\). Therefore the rejection probability conditioned on column _i_ equals the fraction of _disagreeing_ edges of _G_ under the labeling _g<sub>i</sub>_:

\(\rho_i:=\mathbf{Pr}\left[T\mathrm{rejects}|i\right]=\frac{1}{|E|}\sum_{(u,v)\in E}\mathbf{1}\big[g_i(u)\neq g_i(v)\big].\)

We now relate \(\rho_i\) to \(\Delta_i\) using the expansion of _G_. Let \(\pi\) be the uniform distribution on \(A\cup B\), and write \(\langle f,h\rangle:=\mathbb{E}_{v\sim\pi}[f(v)h(v)]\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(f):=\langle f-\mathbb{E}[f],f-\mathbb{E}[f]\rangle\). Let _P_ be the random-walk operator on _G_ (normalized adjacency).

Apply Lemma 4.5 to \(f=g_i\in\{0,1\}^{A\cup B}\). Then \(\rho_i=\frac{1}{|E|}\sum_{(u,v)}\mathbf{1}[g_i(u)\neq g_i(v)]=\frac{1}{|E|}\sum_{(u,v)}(g_i(u)-g_i(v))^2\), so<tbc>

\(\rho_i\ge 2(1-\sigma(G))\mathrm{Var}(g_i).\)

<tbc>For a {0,1}-valued function, \(\mathrm{Var}(g_i)=\theta_i(1-\theta_i)\) where \(\theta_i\) is the fraction of 1’s; moreover \(\Delta_i=\mathrm{min}\{\theta_i,1-\theta_i\}\le\frac{1}{2}\), hence \(\theta_i(1-\theta_i)\ge\frac{1}{2}\Delta_i\). Therefore,<tbc>

\(\rho_i\ge(1-\sigma(G))\Delta_i.\)

<tbc>Averaging over the random column _i_ yields

\(\mathbf{Pr}\left[T\mathrm{rejects}y\right]=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^k\rho_i\ge(1-\sigma(G))\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i=(1-\sigma(G))\Delta\big(y,\mathrm{Rep}^\pm(k,t)\big),\)

which proves the desired soundness with \(\kappa=1-\sigma(G)\).

(4) _Degree._ Each vertex of _G_ has exactly _d_ incident edges, so a coordinate (_v,i_) appears in exactly _d_ possible queries. This _d_ is fixed once we choose _G_ and does not depend on _t_ or _n_.

Using any constant-degree bipartite expander family (e.g., Ramanujan graphs), \(\sigma(G)\le 2\sqrt{d-1}/d\), hence \(\kappa\ge 1-2\sqrt{d-1}/d\) is a positive constant.

## 5 Maximum _k_-Coverage

We show how the sensitivity lower bound for Max E3SAT implies a matching bound for the maximum _k_-coverage problem when algorithms achieve near-perfect coverage on perfectly coverable instances.

In the maximum _k_-coverage problem, an instance _I_=(_U,_F) has a universe _U_ and a family \(\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^U\). Outputs are _k_-subfamilies \(\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\) encoded by their indicator vectors \(\unknown_\mathcal{S}\in\{0,1\}^\mathcal{F}\), and we measure distances with the Hamming metric \(d_\mathrm{H}(\unknown_\mathcal{S},\unknown_{\mathcal{S}^\prime})=|\mathcal{S}\triangle\mathcal{S}'|\). Two instances are neighbors if they differ only in the incidence vector of a single element \(e\in U\): equivalently, we delete _e_ and insert a fresh element whose membership across F can be chosen arbitrarily.

### 5.1 Max E3SAT

In Max E3SAT, an instance \(\Phi=(V,\{0,1\},\mathcal{C})\) consists of variables _V_ and 3-CNF clauses C={_C_<sub>1</sub>_,...,C<sub>m</sub>_}. The output space is {0,1}_<sup>V</sup>_ equipped with the Hamming metric _d_<sub>H</sub>. Combining the standard reduction from Max E3SAT to Max E3LIN2 with a swapping variant of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 (obtained by adapting its proof to replace clause deletions with clause replacements) yields the following consequence.

**Corollary 5.1.** _There exist constants_ \(\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)\) _and c\>_0 _such that for every randomized Max E3SAT algorithm_ A _that, on every satisfiable instance_ \(\Phi=(V,\{0,1\},\mathcal{C}=\{C_1,\dots,C_m\})\)_, outputs in expectation a_ \((1-\varepsilon_0)\)_-approximate assignment, there is a satisfiable_ \(\Phi\) _with_

\(\mathrm{max}_{i\in[m]}\mathrm{max}_{C^\prime\in\mathcal{L}_i}\mathsf{EMD}_{d_\mathrm{H}}\big(\mathcal{A}(\Phi),\mathcal{A}(\Phi-C_i+C')\big)\ge c|V|.\) (6)

_Here_ L_<sub>i</sub> denotes the set of clauses on the three variables that appear in C<sub>i</sub>, and_ \(\Phi-C_i+C'\) _is the instance obtained from_ \(\Phi\) _by replacing C<sub>i</sub> with_ \(C'\).

## 5.2 Block Gadget Reduction

Fix integers _n_=|_V_| and \(k\le n\). Without loss of generality, we assume that _n_ is divisible by _k_. Partition _V_ into _k_ disjoint blocks \(V=V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k\) with |_V<sub>i</sub>_|=_n/k_. For each \(i\in[k]\) and \(\alpha\in\{0,1\}^{V_i}\) create a set \(S_{i,\alpha}\). Let _m_=|_C_|. Without loss of generality, we assume that _m_ is divisible by _k_. We choose _M=m/k_. For each block _i_, add a multiset _G<sub>i</sub>_ of _M_ new guard elements. \(\big|\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kS_{i,\alpha_i}\right)\cap U_\mathrm{cl}\big|=|\{C_j\in C|x\text{\textit{satisfies}}C_j\}|.\)
