Suppose a k-subfamily_ S _covers at least_ \((1-\varepsilon)|U^+|\) _elements. If_ \(M>\varepsilon|U^+|\)_, then_ S _contains at least one set from each block. As_ |S|=_k, it in fact contains exactly one from every block and therefore covers all guards U_<sub>gd</sub>.

_Proof._ If block _i_ contributes no set, all _M_ guards in _G<sub>i</sub>_ remain uncovered, contradicting \(\big|\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal{S}}S\big|\ge(1-\varepsilon)|U^+|\) when \(M>\varepsilon|U^+|\). With _k_ blocks and budget _k_, covering each block at least once is equivalent to selecting exactly one per block.

### A canonical decoder.

Whenever S contains exactly one set from each block we write it as \(\mathcal{S}=\{S_{i,\alpha_i}\}_{i=1}^k\) and define \(D(\mathcal{S})\in\{0,1\}^V\) to be the concatenation of the block assignments.

**Lemma 5.5** (Decoder Lipschitzness)**.** _Let_ \(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{S}'\) _be k-subfamilies that each contain exactly one set per block. Then_

\(d_\mathrm{H}\big(D(\mathcal{S}),D(\mathcal{S}')\big)\le\frac{n}{2k}\cdot d_\mathrm{H}(\unknown_\mathcal{S},\unknown_{\mathcal{S}^\prime}).\)

_Proof._ Changing the choice within one block removes one set and adds another, increasing the symmetric difference by two. Each affected block modifies at most _n/k_ assignment bits, so the claimed Lipschitz bound follows.

**Lemma 5.6.** _Assume_ S _covers at least_ \((1-\varepsilon)|U^+|\) _elements and, by Lemma 5.4, contains exactly one set per block. Then the decoded assignment x=D_(S) _satisfies at least_ \((1-2\varepsilon)m\) _clauses. In particular, this conclusion holds whenever_ \(M\le m/k\)_, because then_ \(|U^+|=m+Mk\le 2m\) _and all guards are covered._

_Proof._ All _Mk_ guards are covered. Hence the number of covered clause elements is at least \((1-\varepsilon)|U^+|-Mk=(1-\varepsilon)(m+Mk)-Mk=(1-\varepsilon)m-\varepsilon Mk\ge(1-2\varepsilon)m\) whenever \(Mk\le m\). By Lemma 5.2, this equals the number of satisfied clauses.

## 5.3 Sensitivity Transfer

We now relate algorithms for the maximum _k_-coverage problem to algorithms for Max E3SAT.

**Theorem 5.7** (Restatement of Theorem 1.5)**.** _There exists_ \(\varepsilon_0>0\) _such that, for every_ \(\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_0)\) _and every_ \(k<1/(2\varepsilon)\)_, any randomized_ \((1-\varepsilon)\)_-approximation algorithm_ B _for the maximum k- coverage problem (in expectation) has an instance I_<sup>+</sup> _with_ OPT(_I_<sup>+</sup>)=|_U_<sup>+</sup>| _on which_

\(\text{Sens}(\mathcal{B},I^+)=\Omega(k),\)

_with an implicit constant that is universal._

_Proof._ Let \(\varepsilon_0\in(0,1)\) and _c\>_0 be the constants supplied by Corollary 5.1. Fix \(\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_0)\), \(k<1/(2\varepsilon)\), and a randomized \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithm B.

_Step 1: Build an E3SAT algorithm from_ B. Define \(\mathcal{A}_\text{sat}:=D\circ\mathcal{B}\circ R_k^+\) and set _M_:=_m/k_ in the reduction \(R_k^+\).

_Step 2:_ A<sub>sat</sub> _is_ \((1-\varepsilon_0)\)_-accurate on satisfiable inputs._ When \(\Phi\) is satisfiable, choosing the set whose block restriction matches a satisfying assignment yields perfect coverage of \(R_k^+(\Phi)\). Because _M=m/k_ and \(k<1/(2\varepsilon)\), we have \(M>\varepsilon|U^+|\) (indeed \(|U^+|=m+Mk\le 2m\) and \(M\ge m/k>2\varepsilon m\)). Therefore Lemma 5.4 ensures that \(\mathcal{B}(R_k^+(\Phi))\) selects exactly one set per block, and Lemma 5.6 gives that \(D\circ\mathcal{B}(R_k^+(\Phi))\) satisfies at least \((1-2\varepsilon)m\ge(1-\varepsilon_0)m\) clauses in expectation.

_Step 3: Invoke the Max E3SAT sensitivity bound._ We choose \(\varepsilon_0\) to be small enough. Then by (6), there exist a satisfiable \(\Phi\) and a clause \(C'_t\) on the same variable triple as some \(C_t\in\mathcal{C}\) such that the instance \(\Phi':=\Phi-C_t+C'_t\) satisfies

\(\mathsf{EMD}_{d_\text{H}}(\mathcal{A}_\text{sat}(\Phi),\mathcal{A}_\text{sat}(\Phi'))\ge cn,\)

where _n_=|_V_|. Let \(I^+=R_k^+(\Phi)\) and \(I^{+\prime}=R_k^+(\Phi')\). By Lemma 5.3, \(I^{+\prime}\) is obtained from _I_<sup>+</sup> by reprogramming the single clause element _e<sub>t</sub>_, so it is a valid neighbor in the maximum _k_-coverage problem.

_Step 4: EMD contraction through the decoder._ Let F<sup>(_k_)</sup> denote the set of _k_-subfamilies of F. Conditioning on the event that B selects exactly one set per block (which holds for both _I_<sup>+</sup> and \(I^{+\prime}\) by the guard argument above), Lemma 5.5 shows that the decoder _D_ is _n/_(2_k_)-Lipschitz from (F<sup>(_k_)</sup>_,d_H) to ({0,1}_<sup>V</sup>,d_H). Let \(D_*\mu\) denote the pushforward of a distribution \(\mu\) under _D_. The Lipschitz contraction property for earthmover distance therefore implies

\(\mathsf{EMD}_{d_\text{H}}(D_*\mathcal{B}(I^+),D_*\mathcal{B}(I^{+\prime}))\le\frac{n}{2k}\cdot\mathsf{EMD}_{d_\text{H}}(\mathcal{B}(I^+),\mathcal{B}(I^{+\prime})).\)

Combining with Step 3 and rearranging gives \(\mathsf{EMD}_{d_\text{H}}(\mathcal{B}(I^+),\mathcal{B}(I^{+\prime}))\ge\Omega(k)\), which is precisely \(\text{Sens}(\mathcal{B},I^+)=\Omega(k)\). Because \(R_k^+(\Phi)\) is perfectly coverable, this concludes the promised instance.

## 6 A Boolean-Function View of Randomized Algorithms for Satisfiable Max E3SAT

In this section we recast the instability results from Sections 3.3 and 5.1 in the language of Boolean functions. We study randomized algorithms that, given a satisfiable Max E3SAT formula, output an assignment satisfying almost all clauses in expectation. Our hard instances are not arbitrary unrelated formulas: they form an explicit local subcube inside the ordinary SAT input space, indexed by messages \(m\in\{0,1\}^k\). All formulas in the family share the same variables and the same ordered clause skeleton, and flipping one bit of _m_ changes only _O_(1) clause signs. Once the algorithm’s random seed is fixed, each output bit becomes an ordinary Boolean function of _m_. Its influence is the sum, over all message coordinates, of the probability that flipping that coordinate changes the output bit. The main conclusion is that, on this explicit satisfiable family, these output bits cannot all have small influence: averaged over the random seed, the sum of their influences is necessarily large. This viewpoint is what later yields the junta, pseudo-junta, decision-tree, and bounded-depth circuit corollaries.

We say that a randomized algorithm _A_ is _one-sided_ \((1-\eta)\)-approximate for Max E3SAT if _A_ is defined on every 3-CNF formula and, for every satisfiable input formula \(\Phi\),<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_{a\sim A(\Phi)}\big[\#\text{clauses of}\Phi\text{satisfied by}a\big]\ge(1-\eta)|\Phi|.\)

<tbc>Equivalently, if _R_ denotes the internal random seed of _A_, then

\(\mathbb{E}_R\big[\#\text{clauses of}\Phi\text{satisfied by}A(\Phi;R)\big]\ge(1-\eta)|\Phi|\)

for every satisfiable \(\Phi\). No guarantee is required on unsatisfiable inputs. When _A_ happens to be deterministic, the seed _R_ is trivial and all of the statements below reduce to the deterministic version.

### The standard formula encoding.

Fix integers _n_ and _M_, and regard a 3-CNF formula on variable set \[_n_\] with exactly _M_ clauses as an ordered list<tbc>

\(\Phi=(C_1,\dots,C_M).\)

<tbc>Write each clause in the canonical order of its three variable indices, and encode each literal by the binary representation of its variable index in \[_n_\] together with one sign bit indicating whether it is negated. Let

\(\text{Enc}_{n,M}(\Phi)\in\{0,1\}^N,N:=M\big(3\lceil log_2n\rceil+3\big),\)

denote the concatenation of the _M_ clause encodings. Throughout this section, when we write \(A(\Phi)\) for such a randomized algorithm _A_, we mean the output distribution \(A(\text{Enc}_{n,M}(\Phi))\) under this standard clause-by-clause encoding. Thus the ambient input space is the completely ordinary bit representation of 3-CNF formulas; the parameter \(m\in\{0,1\}^k\) used below merely indexes an explicit hard subfamily inside that ambient space.

### 6.1 From Instability to Influence

We begin with the randomized E3LIN2 instability statement supplied by the LTC framework.

**Lemma 6.1.** _There exist constants_ \(\eta_\mathrm{lin},c_\mathrm{lin}>0\) _and an explicit family_ \(\{I(m)\}_{m\in\{0,1\}^k}\) _of satisfiable bounded-occurrence Max E3LIN2 instances on_ \(n=\Theta(k)\) _variables such that every randomized algorithm B satisfying_<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_R\big[\#\text{\textit{equations of}}I(m)\text{\textit{satisfied by}}B(I(m);R)\big]\ge(1-\eta_\mathrm{lin})|I(m)|\forall m\in\{0,1\}^k\)

<tbc>_obeys_

\(\mathbb{E}_{m\in\{0,1\}^k}\mathbb{E}_{i\in[k]}\big[\text{EMD}_{d_\mathrm{H}}\big(B(I(m)),B(I(m^{\oplus i}))\big)\big]\ge c_\mathrm{lin}n,\)

_where_ \(m^{\oplus i}\) _denotes m with its ith bit flipped._

_Proof._ This is exactly the averaged earth-mover lower bound obtained from Lemma 3.7 using the binary LRCC family from Section 4.1. Since the rate, distance, detection probability, and variable degree are all absolute constants, the right-hand side of Lemma 3.7 is bounded below by a positive constant for sufficiently small \(\eta_\mathrm{lin}\). Multiplying by the block length converts the normalized Hamming metric to _d_<sub>H</sub>, and the resulting Max E3LIN2 instances have \(\Theta(n)\) output coordinates. Hence the averaged instability is \(\Omega(n)\).

We now pass from E3LIN2 to E3SAT using the standard four-clause gadget. Because the E3LIN2 family already comes with a fixed ordered list of equation scopes, this step preserves a common template: varying _m_ changes only the right-hand-side bits of _O_(1) equations, hence only the sign patterns in _O_(1) gadgets. For each equation

\(x\oplus y\oplus z=b,\)

let _G<sub>b</sub>(x,y,z_) denote the standard 4-clause gadget on the same variable triple with the property that any assignment satisfies all four clauses iff it satisfies the equation, and otherwise it satisfies exactly three clauses.

**Theorem 6.2** (One-sided endpoint instability for ordinarily encoded satisfiable Max E3SAT)**.** _There exist constants_ \(\eta,c,\Delta>0\)_, an integer L=O_(1)_, and an explicit family_ \(\{\Phi(m)\}_{m\in\{0,1\}^k}\) _of satisfiable bounded-occurrence_ 3_-CNF formulas on the same variable set_ \[_n_\] _with the same number M=O(n_) _of clauses, where_ \(n=\Theta(k)\)_, such that the following holds._

_Let A be any randomized algorithm that is one-sided_ \((1-\eta)\)_-approximate for Max E3SAT. Then:_

1. **_Endpoint instability._**<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathbb{E}_{m\in\{0,1\}^k}\mathbb{E}_{i\in[k]}\big[\text{EMD}_{d_\mathrm{H}}\big(A(\Phi(m)),A(\Phi(m^{\oplus i}))\big)\big]\ge cn.\)<tbc>

_2._ **_Single-clause path version._** _For every_ \(m\in\{0,1\}^k\) _and_ \(i\in[k]\)_, there exists a sequence_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\Phi(m)=\Psi_0^{m,i},\Psi_1^{m,i},\dots,\Psi_L^{m,i}=\Phi(m^{\oplus i})\)<tbc>

<tbc>_such that each consecutive pair_ \(\Psi_{t-1}^{m,i},\Psi_t^{m,i}\) _differs by replacing a single clause by another clause on the same variable triple, and_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathbb{E}_{m\in\{0,1\}^k}\mathbb{E}_{i\in[k]}\big[\sum_{t=1}^L\text{EMD}_{d_\mathrm{H}}\big(A(\Psi_{t-1}^{m,i}),A(\Psi_t^{m,i})\big)\big]\ge cn.\)<tbc>

_Moreover, the hard family is local inside the ordinary SAT input space: for every_ \(m\in\{0,1\}^k\) _and_ \(i\in[k]\),

\(d_\mathrm{H}\big(\mathrm{Enc}_{n,M}(\Phi(m)),\mathrm{Enc}_{n,M}(\Phi(m^{\oplus i}))\big)\le\Delta,\)

_and each adjacent pair_ \(\Psi_{t-1}^{m,i},\Psi_t^{m,i}\) _in item 2 differs in at most three input bits under_ Enc<sub>_n,M_</sub>_. In particular, the second statement is_ one-sided: _only the endpoint formulas_ \(\Phi(m)\) _and_ \(\Phi(m^{\oplus i})\) _are required to be satisfiable; the intermediate formulas_ \(\Psi_t^{m,i}\) _may be arbitrary._

_Proof._ Let \(\{I(m)\}_{m\in\{0,1\}^k}\) be the satisfiable Max E3LIN2 family from Lemma 6.1. For each _m_, define \(\Phi(m)\) by replacing every equation of _I(m_) with the corresponding four-clause gadget. Order the clauses of \(\Phi(m)\) by first fixing the order of the E3LIN2 constraints and then, inside each gadget, fixing the order of its four clauses. The key point is that this ordered list of equation scopes is independent of _m_; only the right-hand-side bits vary with the message. Because the reduction is local and each variable appears in only constantly many equations in the E3LIN2 family, the resulting formulas are explicit, satisfiable, and bounded-occurrence, with _M=O(n_) clauses.

Set \(\eta:=\eta_\mathrm{lin}/4\), and let _A_ be a randomized one-sided \((1-\eta)\)-approximate algorithm for Max E3SAT. Define<tbc>

\(B(I(m)):=A(\Phi(m)).\)

<tbc>Let _Y_ be a random assignment drawn from \(A(\Phi(m))\), and let _s(Y_) denote the number of E3LIN2 equations of _I(m_) satisfied by _Y_ . Since each satisfied equation contributes 4 satisfied clauses and each unsatisfied equation contributes exactly 3, we have<tbc>

\(\#\text{clauses of}\Phi(m)\text{satisfied by}Y=3|I(m)|+s(Y).\)

<tbc>Therefore

\(\mathbb{E}[s(Y)]\ge(1-\eta)4|I(m)|-3|I(m)|=(1-4\eta)|I(m)|=(1-\eta_\mathrm{lin})|I(m)|.\)

Thus _B_ satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma 6.1, and item 1 follows immediately with _c_:=_c_<sub>lin</sub>.

It remains to justify the locality claims in the standard SAT input encoding. By construction of the LTC-induced E3LIN2 family, the two instances _I(m_) and \(I(m^{\oplus i})\) differ only on those local tests that read the _i_th message coordinate, hence on at most \(\theta\) equations, where \(\theta=O(1)\) is the variable degree of the tester. For every fixed equation slot, the three variables appearing in that equation are independent of _m_; only the right-hand-side bit may change with _m_. Consequently, when such an equation is replaced by the corresponding E3SAT gadget, all variable-index bits in the standard clause-listing encoding remain fixed, and only the sign bits of the literals may change. Each changed equation slot affects four clauses, each clause contributes three sign bits, and therefore

\(d_\mathrm{H}\big(\mathrm{Enc}_{n,M}(\Phi(m)),\mathrm{Enc}_{n,M}(\Phi(m^{\oplus i}))\big)\le\Delta:=12\theta.\)

This proves the bounded-difference claim for the endpoints.

For item 2, fix _m_ and _i_. Changing one E3LIN2 equation changes one four-clause gadget, and that gadget change can be implemented by four single-clause replacements. Since the source and target clauses in each such replacement use the same variable triple, their standard encodings differ only in the three sign bits of that clause. Therefore there is a sequence

\(\Phi(m)=\Psi_0^{m,i},\Psi_1^{m,i},\dots,\Psi_L^{m,i}=\Phi(m^{\oplus i})\)

of length at most \(L:=4\theta\) in which each step replaces a single clause by another clause on the same variable triple. (If a shorter path exists, pad it with repeated endpoint formulas.) By the triangle<tbc>

inequality for EMD<sub>_d_<sub>H</sub></sub>,

\(\text{EMD}_{d_\mathrm{H}}\big(A(\Phi(m)),A(\Phi(m^{\oplus i}))\big)\le\sum_{t=1}^L\text{EMD}_{d_\mathrm{H}}\big(A(\Psi_{t-1}^{m,i}),A(\Psi_t^{m,i})\big).\)

Averaging over _m_ and _i_ and using item 1 completes the proof.

## The hard embedding is itself simple.

Define the explicit input embedding

\(x(m):=\mathrm{Enc}_{n,M}(\Phi(m))\in\{0,1\}^N.\)

Each output bit of _x_ is either a fixed variable-index bit or a sign bit of a clause in one gadget, and the sign pattern of that gadget is determined by a single local E3LIN2 test. Since the tester query complexity is constant, each output bit of _x_ depends on only _O_(1) message coordinates. Thus _x_ is computable by a linear-size _NC_<sup>0</sup> circuit. This is important for the randomized circuit corollary below: the hardness is not coming from a complicated front end, but from the randomized algorithm itself.

Because the relevant input family and output space are finite, any such randomized algorithm can be realized on a common finite probability space. We therefore fix a random seed _R_ and a realization \(A(\cdot;R)\) whose law is \(A(\cdot)\) on every input. For the rest of the section write<tbc>

\(F_R(m):=A(x(m);R)=\big(f_{1,R}(m),\dots,f_{n,R}(m)\big)\in\{0,1\}^n.\)

<tbc>For each fixed seed _r_ and output coordinate _v_, the slice \(f_{v,r}:\{0,1\}^k\rightarrow\{0,1\}\) is an ordinary Boolean function. For a Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^k\rightarrow\{0,1\}\), write<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Inf}(f):=\sum_{i=1}^k\mathbf{Pr}_{m\in\{0,1\}^k}\big[f(m)\neq f(m^{\oplus i})\big].\)

<tbc>We call

\(\mathrm{SCInf}(A):=\mathbb{E}_R\big[\sum_{v=1}^n\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,R})\big]\)

the _seed-averaged cumulative influence_ of the pullback of _A_ to the hard family. When _A_ is deterministic, this is exactly the ordinary cumulative influence from the deterministic version of the section.

## Why the pullback is the right object.

The theorem above is already stated in the standard formula-input model. We pass to the cube coordinates \(m\in\{0,1\}^k\) because the classical structural results we want to invoke, i.e., junta theorems, pseudo-junta theorems, and average-sensitivity upper bounds for bounded-depth circuits and formulas, are formulated for Boolean functions on product spaces. Moreover, by Theorem 6.2, adjacent points of the hard cube map to formulas whose standard encodings differ in only _O_(1) bits, so the pullback does not create artificial hardness: it is simply a convenient coordinate system for an explicit, genuinely local subfamily of ordinary SAT inputs. The role of the random seed is only to turn the randomized algorithm into deterministic slices to which these classical Boolean-function bounds apply.

**Corollary 6.3** (Seed-averaged cumulative influence)**.** _Under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.2, every randomized algorithm A that is one-sided_ \((1-\eta)\)_-approximate for Max E3SAT satisfies_<tbc>

\(\mathrm{SCInf}(A)=\mathbb{E}_R\big[\sum_{v=1}^n\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,R})\big]=\Omega(nk).\)

<tbc>_Moreover, for the single-clause paths from Theorem 6.2,_<tbc>

\(\sum_{v=1}^n\sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{t=1}^L\mathbf{Pr}_{m,R}\big[A(\Psi_{t-1}^{m,i};R)_v\neq A(\Psi_t^{m,i};R)_v\big]=\Omega(nk).\)

<tbc>_Proof._ For the endpoint statement, couple the two output distributions _A(x(m_)) and \(A(x(m^{\oplus i}))\) by using the same random seed _R_ on both inputs. This is a valid coupling, so<tbc>

\(\mathrm{EMD}_{d_\mathrm{H}}\big(A(x(m)),A(x(m^{\oplus i}))\big)\le\mathbb{E}_R\big[d_\mathrm{H}\big(F_R(m),F_R(m^{\oplus i})\big)\big].\)

<tbc>Averaging over _m_ and _i_ gives<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_{m,i}\big[\mathrm{EMD}_{d_\mathrm{H}}\big(A(x(m)),A(x(m^{\oplus i}))\big)\big]\le\mathbb{E}_{m,i,R}\big[d_\mathrm{H}\big(F_R(m),F_R(m^{\oplus i})\big)\big].\)

<tbc>Expanding Hamming distance coordinatewise and then unfolding the definition of total influence,<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_{m,i,R}\big[d_\mathrm{H}\big(F_R(m),F_R(m^{\oplus i})\big)\big]=\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{E}_R\big[\sum_{v=1}^n\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,R})\big].\)

<tbc>Applying item 1 of Theorem 6.2 yields

\(\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{E}_R\big[\sum_{v=1}^n\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,R})\big]=\Omega(n),\)

which is equivalent to the displayed lower bound.

The path version is identical: for each _m,i,t_,

\(\mathrm{EMD}_{d_\mathrm{H}}\big(A(\Psi_{t-1}^{m,i}),A(\Psi_t^{m,i})\big)\le\mathbb{E}_R\big[d_\mathrm{H}\big(A(\Psi_{t-1}^{m,i};R),A(\Psi_t^{m,i};R)\big)\big],\)

and summing over _t_, averaging over _m_ and _i_, and expanding coordinatewise proves the second claim.

**Corollary 6.4** (Many highly influential output coordinates on average over the seed)**.** _There exist constants_ \(\alpha,\gamma>0\) _such that_<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_R\big[\big|\{v\in[n]:\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,R})\ge\alpha k\}\big|\big]\ge\gamma n.\)

<tbc>_In particular, for at least one choice of the internal randomness r, at least_ \(\gamma n\) _output coordinates satisfy_

\(\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,r})\ge\alpha k.\)

_Hence on at least one seed slice, linearly many output coordinates depend on_ \(\Omega(k)\) _message coordinates and have deterministic decision-tree depth_ \(\Omega(k)\).

_Proof._ By Corollary 6.3, there exists a constant _c_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0 such that<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_R\big[\sum_{v=1}^n\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,R})\big]\ge c_0nk.\)

<tbc>Set \(\alpha:=c_0/2\), and for each seed _r_ define<tbc>

\(H_r:=\{v\in[n]:\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,r})\ge\alpha k\}.\)

<tbc>Since \(\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,r})\le k\) for every _v_ and _r_,<tbc>

\(\sum_{v=1}^n\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,r})\le|H_r|k+(n-|H_r|)\alpha k.\)

<tbc>Taking expectations over _R_ and rearranging shows that

\(\mathbb{E}_R[|H_R|]\ge\gamma n\)

for some constant \(\gamma>0\).

If a Boolean function depends on at most _T_ input coordinates, then its total influence is at most _T_. Likewise, the deterministic decision-tree depth _D(f_) satisfies \(\mathrm{Inf}(f)\le D(f)\). Therefore every coordinate counted by _H<sub>r</sub>_ depends on \(\Omega(k)\) message bits and has decision-tree depth \(\Omega(k)\).

## 6.2 A Meta-Corollary for Low-Influence Representation Classes

For a class G_<sub>k</sub>_ of Boolean functions on {0,1}_<sup>k</sup>_, define<tbc>

\(\mathrm{dist}(f,\mathcal{G}_k):=\mathrm{inf}_{g\in\mathcal{G}_k}\mathbf{Pr}_{m\in\{0,1\}^k}\big[f(m)\neq g(m)\big].\)

<tbc>**Corollary 6.5** (A meta-corollary for randomized low-influence classes)**.** _Let_ \(\alpha,\gamma>0\) _be the constants from Corollary 6.4. Let_ G_<sub>k</sub> be any class of Boolean functions on_ {0,1}_<sup>k</sup> satisfying_<tbc>

\(\mathrm{sup}_{g\in\mathcal{G}_k}\mathrm{Inf}(g)\le\beta(k).\)

<tbc>_If_ \(\beta(k)\le\alpha k/2\)_, then_<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_R\big[\big|\{v\in[n]:\mathrm{dist}(f_{v,R},\mathcal{G}_k)\ge\alpha/4\}\big|\big]\ge\gamma n.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ For any two Boolean functions \(f,g:\{0,1\}^k\rightarrow\{0,1\}\),<tbc>

\(\big|\mathrm{Inf}(f)-\mathrm{Inf}(g)\big|\le 2k\mathbf{Pr}_{m\in\{0,1\}^k}\big[f(m)\neq g(m)\big].\)

<tbc>Indeed, for each \(i\in[k]\),

\(\big|\mathbf{Pr}_m\big[f(m)\neq f(m^{\oplus i})\big]-\mathbf{Pr}_m\big[g(m)\neq g(m^{\oplus i})\big]\big|\le 2\mathbf{Pr}_m\big[f(m)\neq g(m)\big],\)

and summing over _i_ proves the claim.

Now fix a seed _r_ and let _v_ be any coordinate with \(\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,r})\ge\alpha k\). For every \(g\in\mathcal{G}_k\) we then have<tbc>

\(\mathbf{Pr}_m\big[f_{v,r}(m)\neq g(m)\big]\ge\frac{\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,r})-\mathrm{Inf}(g)}{2k}\ge\frac{\alpha k-\beta(k)}{2k}\ge\alpha/4.\)

<tbc>Thus

\(\big|\{v\in[n]:\mathrm{dist}(f_{v,r},\mathcal{G}_k)\ge\alpha/4\}\big|\ge\big|\{v\in[n]:\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,r})\ge\alpha k\}\big|.\)

Taking expectations over _R_ and applying Corollary 6.4 proves the displayed lower bound. The final sentence is immediate.

The strength of Corollary 6.5 is that it turns Corollary 6.3 into a black-box lower-bound principle: _any_ coordinatewise representation class whose seedwise realizations have sublinear total influence is automatically ruled out on linearly many output coordinates on average over the seed. The next three subsections record concrete instantiations.

## 6.3 Anti-Junta and Anti-Pseudo-Junta Consequences

Recall that a Boolean function on {0,1}_<sup>k</sup>_ is a _K-junta_ if it depends on at most _K_ input coordinates. We also use Hatami’s notion of a _K-pseudo-junta_ \[28\], which generalizes juntas by allowing the relevant coordinates to vary with the input in a structured way. We will not need the full formal definition here; the only property used below is that every _K_-pseudo-junta has total influence at most 2_K_.

**Corollary 6.6** (On average over the seed, linearly many outputs are far from juntas and pseudo-juntas)**.** _There exist constants_ \(\gamma,\delta>0\) _such that the following holds for all sufficiently large k._

1. _For every_ \(K\le\gamma k\)_, one has_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathbb{E}_R\left[\left|\{v\in[n]:\mathrm{dist}(f_{v,R},\{K\text{\textit{-juntas}}\})\ge\delta\}\right|\right]\ge\delta n.\)<tbc>

_2._ _For every_ \(K\le\gamma k\)_, one has_

<tbc>\(\mathbb{E}_R\left[\left|\{v\in[n]:\mathrm{dist}(f_{v,R},\{K\text{\textit{-pseudo-juntas}}\})\ge\delta\}\right|\right]\ge\delta n.\)

_Proof._ Let \(\alpha_0,\gamma_0\) be the constants from Corollary 6.4. Every _K_-junta satisfies \(\mathrm{Inf}(g)\le K\) \[16\], and every _K_-pseudo-junta satisfies \(\mathrm{Inf}(g)\le 2K\) by Hatami’s proposition on pseudo-juntas \[28\]. Thus both claims follow from Corollary 6.5 by taking \(\delta:=\mathrm{min}\{\alpha_0/4,\gamma_0\}\) and shrinking the displayed constant \(\gamma\) by an absolute factor if needed so that both _K_ and 2_K_ are at most \(\alpha_0k/2\).

The point of Corollary 6.6 is that the randomized task of finding near-satisfying assignments for an explicit satisfiable Max E3SAT family forces averaged non-junta structure: linearly many output coordinates stay a constant distance away from every small junta and every small pseudo-junta on average over the internal randomness.

## 6.4 Decision Trees and Local Dependence

For a Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^k\rightarrow\{0,1\}\), let _D(f_) denote its deterministic decision-tree depth, that is, the minimum worst-case number of input bits that must be queried in order to determine _f(m_).

**Corollary 6.7** (On average over the seed, linearly many outputs have linear decision-tree depth)**.** _There exist constants_ \(\alpha,\gamma>0\) _such that_

\(\mathbb{E}_R\left[\left|\{v\in[n]:D(f_{v,R})\ge\alpha k\}\right|\right]\ge\gamma n,\)

_Equivalently, averaged over the internal randomness of the algorithm, linearly many output coordinates cannot be computed by reading o(k_) _message bits._

_Proof._ The inequality \(\mathrm{Inf}(f)\le D(f)\) is classical for Boolean functions; see, for example, Rossman’s discussion of formula average sensitivity \[41\]. Therefore every coordinate counted in Corollary 6.4 also has decision-tree depth \(\Omega(k)\).

What is new here is an explicit satisfiable bounded-occurrence family for which, even allowing internal randomness and approximation in expectation, linearly many seedwise output bits have linear deterministic query complexity with respect to the message coordinates, on average over the seed. This contrasts with local-access results that achieve polylogarithmic query complexity under strong LLL-type sparsity assumptions or in the high-_k_/low-degree regime \[13, 42\].

## 6.5 Constant-Depth Circuits and s

We now record a bounded-depth consequence. Boppana’s average-sensitivity bound for constant- depth circuits and Rossman’s strengthening for bounded-depth formulas place polynomial-size bounded-depth computation in the low-influence regime on the message cube \[5, 41\]. Since our hard family is embedded into the standard SAT encoding by a linear-size _NC_<sup>0</sup> map, the same barrier transfers to randomized bounded-depth computation for finding near-satisfying assignments on satisfiable Max E3SAT instances.

**Corollary 6.8** (No polynomial-size constant-depth randomized circuits for finding near-satisfying assignments)**.** _Fix the standard binary encoding of_ 3_-CNF formulas with n variables and M clauses. Then there is no randomized polynomial-size constant-depth circuit family that, on every satisfiable input formula of this size, outputs in expectation a_ \((1-\eta)\)_-approximate assignment. The same holds for randomized bounded-depth formula families._

_More quantitatively, for every fixed depth D, any such depth-D randomized circuit family must have size_ \(\mathrm{exp}\big(n^{\Omega_D(1)}\big)\).

_Proof._ Suppose there were such a randomized polynomial-size constant-depth circuit family for the encoded 3-CNF inputs. Write it as a deterministic circuit family<tbc>

\(C_{n,M}(x,r)\)

<tbc>with an explicit random seed _r_, and let _A_ denote the induced output distribution when _r_ is sampled uniformly. Composing with the hard embedding<tbc>

\(m\longmapsto x(m)=\mathrm{Enc}_{n,M}(\Phi(m))\)

<tbc>yields, for each fixed seed _r_, a deterministic polynomial-size constant-depth multi-output circuit<tbc>

\(F_r(m)=\big(f_{1,r}(m),\dots,f_{n,r}(m)\big)\)

<tbc>on the message cube, because _x_ is computable by a linear-size _NC_<sup>0</sup> circuit. (The same substitution argument applies to formulas.) By Corollary 6.3, one has<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_R\big[\sum_{v=1}^n\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,R})\big]=\Omega(nk).\)

<tbc>On the other hand, Boppana’s average-sensitivity upper bound for bounded-depth circuits and Rossman’s strengthening for bounded-depth formulas imply that every output bit of a polynomial- size constant-depth circuit or formula has sublinear influence on {0,1}_<sup>k</sup>_, uniformly over the fixed seed _r_ \[5, 41\]. Hence<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_R\big[\sum_{v=1}^n\mathrm{Inf}(f_{v,R})\big]=o(nk),\)

<tbc>contradicting Corollary 6.3 for all sufficiently large _n_. The quantitative lower bound follows from the quantitative form of the same average-sensitivity upper bounds.

The point of Corollary 6.8 is that the obstruction already appears for randomized generation of near-satisfying assignments on satisfiable SAT formulas. Even though each satisfiable instance has many acceptable nearly optimal assignments and the algorithm may use internal randomness, the seedwise output bits still accumulate linear total influence on the hard family, and this rules out the usual polynomial-size bounded-depth circuit and formula classes.

It suffices to exhibit an encoder _f_ whose image is _C_ and whose message coordinates appear in fixed positions after a permutation of coordinates. Since _C_ is linear, \(C=M\mathbb{F}_p^k\) for some \(M\in\mathbb{F}_p^{n\times k}\) of rank _k_. By the definition of rank, there exists a set of indices \(I=\{i_1,i_2,\dots,i_k\}\subseteq[n]\) such that the rows of _M_ indexed by _I_ span \(\mathbb{F}_p^k\). Let \(\Pi\in\mathbb{F}_p^{n\times n}\) be the permutation matrix that moves the coordinates in _I_ to the first _k_ positions and let \(\widetilde{M}:=\Pi M\). The first _k_ rows of \(\widetilde{M}\) span \(\mathbb{F}_p^k\), so the projection matrix \(P\in\mathbb{F}_p^{k\times n}\) onto those rows satisfies that \(P\widetilde{M}\) is invertible. Define \(\tilde{f}(m):=\widetilde{M}(P\widetilde{M})^{-1}m\) for \(m\in\mathbb{F}_p^k\). We have

1. \(\tilde{f}(\mathbb{F}_p^k)=\widetilde{M}\mathbb{F}_p^k=\Pi C\);<tbc>

2. The first _k_ coordinates of \(\tilde{f}(m)\) equal \(P\tilde{f}(m)=P\widetilde{M}(P\widetilde{M})^{-1}m=m\).<tbc>

<tbc>Thus \(\tilde{f}\) is a systematic encoder for the permuted code \(\Pi C\), witnessing that \(\Pi C\) is systematic with the same parameters. Undoing the permutation shows that _C_ becomes systematic after the fixed coordinate permutation \(\Pi\), as claimed.
